paragraphs.heading: What nucleic acids are
paragraphs.text: Nucleic acids are large biological molecules found in every cell and every virus. They are linear polymers: chains built from small units called nucleotides. The name covers the two main kinds, DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid). Which kind you get depends on the sugar in the chain: ribose gives RNA, and deoxyribose, a variant of ribose, gives DNA.

paragraphs.heading: What they do
paragraphs.text: Their job is information. They make up genetic material, and in every living cell they create, encode and store information, which they then send and express inside and outside the cell nucleus. DNA and RNA both play a central part in directing how proteins are made. In DNA, the order of base pairs keeps coded instructions in the form of genes. In RNA, base-pair sequences help produce new proteins, which determine most of the chemistry of life.

paragraphs.heading: The building block
paragraphs.text: Each nucleotide has three parts: a five-carbon sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. The phosphate is what makes the molecule acidic. A base joined to a sugar, without the phosphate, is called a nucleoside. Along the chain, sugars and phosphates alternate to form a backbone held together by phosphodiester links. The phosphates attach at the sugar's 3' and 5' carbons, which gives each strand a direction, with a 5' end and a 3' end.

paragraphs.heading: DNA and RNA side by side
paragraphs.text: The sugar differs: DNA has 2'-deoxyribose and RNA has ribose, and the only gap between them is one hydroxyl group. Adenine, cytosine and guanine occur in both, but thymine is found only in DNA and uracil only in RNA. In most natural cases DNA is double-stranded, a chain of base pairs, while RNA is single-stranded, a chain of single bases. There are plenty of exceptions: some viruses carry double-stranded RNA or single-stranded DNA, and structures with three or four strands can sometimes form.

paragraphs.heading: Everywhere, and enormous
paragraphs.text: They take their name from being found first in the nucleus and from their phosphate groups, which relate to phosphoric acid. They are now known in all life forms, including bacteria, archaea, mitochondria, chloroplasts and viruses. Living cells hold both DNA and RNA, apart from some cells such as mature red blood cells, while a virus usually has one or the other. DNA molecules are probably the largest single molecules known. Well-studied examples range from small interfering RNA, 21 nucleotides long, up to human chromosome 1, one molecule with 247 million base pairs.

paragraphs.heading: How they were found
paragraphs.text: Friedrich Miescher partly discovered nucleic acid in 1869 at the University of Tübingen, calling his new substance nuclein. In the early 1880s Albrecht Kossel purified it further, found it to be highly acidic, and later identified the bases. Richard Altmann coined the term nucleic acid in 1889, when DNA and RNA were not yet told apart. Astbury and Bell put out DNA's first X-ray diffraction pattern in 1938. In 1944 the Avery–MacLeod–McCarty experiment showed DNA carries genetic information, and in 1953 Watson and Crick proposed its double helix.
